think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 30-year-old East African man followed for established ankylosing spondylitis presents with acute constrictive chest pain, elevated troponin, and pericarditic ST elevations. The initial diagnostic imperative is ruling out acute myocardial infarction. Furthermore, persistent constitutional inflammatory activity in an established ankylosing spondylitis patient raises the possibility of an underlying systemic process. Disseminated tuberculosis mimicking ankylosing spondylitis with bilateral sacroiliitis, pulmonary lesions, and multichamber lymphadenopathy creates an extraordinary clinical mimicry.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage terminates after emergency cardiopulmonary evaluation, ECG, cardiac echocardiography, routine labs, and plain chest radiography rule out myocardial infarction, immediately prior to whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT, tuberculin skin testing, and bronchoscopy with biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute myocardial infarction presents with ischemic ECG changes and segmental wall motion abnormalities, whereas this patient had diffuse concave ST elevations with PR depression, a normal echocardiogram, and rapid troponin resolution consistent with acute pericarditis. Ankylosing spondylitis explains inflammatory back pain and radiographic sacroiliitis, but extensive hypermetabolic multichamber lymphadenopathy, pulmonary consolidation, and necrotizing granulomas confirm an infectious granulomatous disease. Lymphoma produces multi-station FDG-avid lymphadenopathy but demonstrates clonal malignant lymphoid infiltrates rather than necrotizing granulomas.
case_prompt:
A 30-year-old man of East African origin presents to the emergency department with acute constrictive chest pain. His past medical history is notable for acute methanol intoxication resulting in bilateral permanent blindness due to necrosis in the bilateral putamen. He has been followed in the rheumatology outpatient clinic for ankylosing spondylitis, diagnosed based on a one-year history of inflammatory low back pain with a good clinical response to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and computed tomography demonstrating bilateral grade 2 sacroiliitis. He reports occasional alcohol consumption with no history of tobacco or illicit drug use.

On physical examination, he is in satisfactory general condition, afebrile, with normal vital signs. Examination reveals synovitis of both knees. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal.

Initial laboratory investigations show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 80 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 5.8 mg/dL, moderate hepatic cytolysis (<2 times upper limit of normal), and anicteric cholestasis. Complete blood count, total bilirubin, and renal function are normal. Cardiac troponin is initially 0.091 mg/dL, decreasing to 0.023 mg/dL after 3 hours. Plain chest radiography reveals no abnormalities. An electrocardiogram demonstrates widespread concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression in leads II and III. Bedside transthoracic echocardiography is normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute coronary syndrome was considered due to constrictive chest pain and elevated initial troponin, but excluded by diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression, normal echocardiography, and a rapid decrease in troponin levels.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Troponin level was initially increased to 0.091 mg/dL; it decreased after 3 hours to 0.023 mg/dL. Chest radiography revealed no abnormalities. An electrocardiogram revealed widespread concave S-T elevation and a P-R depression (D2 D3). Cardiac echography was normal. Myocardial infarction was ruled out

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The patient carried an established diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis based on chronic inflammatory back pain, bilateral sacroiliitis, and knee synovitis; however, marked systemic inflammation, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary condensation indicated an infectious granulomatous mimic rather than pure spondyloarthropathy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient reported low inflammatory back pain for more than one year, good response to nonsteroid anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and computer tomography imaging (CT) of bilateral sacroiliitis (grade 2), leading to the diagnosis of AS according to the ASAS criteria... The 18F-FDG-PET/CT revealed mediastinal, hilar pulmonary, supraclavicular and cervical bilateral hypermetabolic lymph nodes, hypermetabolic condensation in the right lung, multiple hypermetabolic lesions of axial skeleton

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Whole-body PET/CT displaying diffuse hypermetabolic mediastinal, hilar, supraclavicular, and cervical lymphadenopathy with skeletal and pulmonary lesions strongly raised suspicion for lymphoma, but pulmonary biopsy demonstrated necrotic granulomas and mycobacteria.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The 18F-FDG-PET/CT revealed mediastinal, hilar pulmonary, supraclavicular and cervical bilateral hypermetabolic lymph nodes, hypermetabolic condensation in the right lung, multiple hypermetabolic lesions of axial skeleton (Figure 2(a)), in particular the thoracic spine, rib cage, and bilateral sacroiliac joints (Figure 3). This was suggestive of either DT or lymphoma... Histological analysis of the lesions showed the presence of necrotic granuloma, and microbiological examination revealed mycobacterium tuberculosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT showing diffuse hypermetabolic lymphadenopathy, pulmonary condensation, and axial lesions, combined with a strongly positive tuberculin skin test (22 x 27 mm) and bronchoscopic biopsy showing necrotizing granulomas with microbiological isolation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, confirmed disseminated tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A tuberculin skin test was done and was highly positive (22 x 27 mm)... Bronchoscopy with biopsy of the right pulmonary lesion was performed. Histological analysis of the lesions showed the presence of necrotic granuloma, and microbiological examination revealed mycobacterium tuberculosis. The diagnosis of DT with axial skeleton, lung, and lymph node involvement was retained

editor_comments: Strict admission breakpoint set before PET/CT, TST, and bronchoscopy. Differential distinctions between myocardial infarction, AS flare, lymphoma, and tuberculosis fully detailed with exact quotes.
